newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian gas muddle requires cash, diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian gas muddle requires cash, diplomacy.

text.p: Sarajevans are shivering in their flats for a fifth winter as Bosnia's government scrambles to come up with the cash needed to buy gas to keep its citizens warm, a British gas expert said on Saturday.

Tony James of Britain's Overseas Development Authority (ODA) in Sarajevo, reported that Bosnia owes a private company in Russia $121 million for gas consumed from the April 1992 start of war here through to the end of October this year.
He said another $47 million worth of gas would be needed to get through the current winter.
Despite not having been paid ,the Russians are still supplying the Bosnian capital with about half the gas it needs.
Government officials, international mediators and experts and supply and distribution experts have been trying to resolve the city's gas problem for weeks.
Bosnian Prime Minister Hasan Muratovic and Swedish mediator Carl Bildt have exchanged harsh words over the city's utility supply situation.
Local authorities have announced they will begin charging households for gas in an effort to raise some of the revenue necessary to pay for supplies.
Observers say that will be easier said than done given the city's war-time history and current poor economic situation.

Although gas supplies were often interrupted by separatist Serbs who laid siege to Sarajevo during the 43-month Bosnian war, the little gas which did get through was provided free to strapped city residents.
"The canton government has a very difficult task enforcing a payment regime in a city which has probably still got 50 per cent refugees and where there's not much work," James said.
"It's a very, very difficult subject to broach when you change from the war-time culture for humanitarian purpose to an out-and-out commercial scenario."
Given that many of the households consuming gas in Sarajevo will not be able to pay, any user-fee scheme is expected to leave a substantial revenue shortfall.
The Bosnian government is hoping the international community can be enticed to help fill that gap even as it negotiates to reschedule payment for gas consumed in past years.

International sources insist there is no truth to rumours that Bosnian Serbs are siphoning gas from the pipeline before it reaches Sarajevo or restricting its flow in some other way, as they did during the war.
